log.msg: Harness live. mlat-runner.mjs spawns claude.exe from a scratch cwd outside the repo, stamps wall-clock time on every stream-json line as it arrives, and writes one row per run to runs.jsonl. Five tasks were written before any run: a one-word reply, the fast-assistant card, read-a-file, write-then-verify, and a hard counting problem whose right answer is 18. Each task carries its rubric, written first.

FIRST BIG FINDING, from two smoke runs: the CLI takes 3.6 to 4.2 seconds to reach its init event, before any API call happens at all. Haiku at low effort answering the word ok: init 3.60 s, first token 4.37 s, finished 4.41 s. The model round trip was 0.8 s; the process start was 3.6 s. Process start, not the model, is what stands between the owner and a card in a couple of seconds.

Prefix measured. The as-launched config loads 90 tools, 57 skills and 4 MCP servers for a 41k-token prefix, and cost 0.0169 USD to say the word ok. The minimal config (strict-mcp-config, no setting sources, an empty tools list, slash commands off, a one-line system prompt) is 823 tokens and 0.0020 USD, and finished 1.1 s sooner.

assign.now: running the cheap pre-reset waves: the card task across Haiku and Sonnet at low, medium and high, plus the config ladder

log.msg: The 3.6 s was an instrument defect, and it is also the single most useful finding so far. The CLI prints to stderr: no stdin data received in 3s, proceeding without it. If you spawn claude -p with stdin left open as a pipe, it waits three seconds for input that never comes before it does anything. Closing stdin (stdio ignore) drops the init event from 3.60 s to 0.59 s and a one-word answer from 4.41 s to 1.45 s. Anyone launching the fast assistant from a script must close or redirect stdin, or three of the owner's couple of seconds are gone before the model is even asked.

Effort is not cosmetic. Same model (Haiku), same card task, same config: low finished in 5.30 s with 1060 thinking tokens, max finished in 14.73 s with about 2.8x the output. The --effort flag reaches the model. Repeats follow; one run each proves only that the knob is connected.

Both xhigh and max are accepted by Haiku without error, so all five levels are legal for every model tested. Every timing taken before this point is discarded and kept as runs-stdinbug.jsonl for the record.

Wave 1 launching: the card task on Haiku and Sonnet at low, medium and high, minimal config, one warm-up plus three timed repeats each. 24 calls, all small prompts, expected under one US dollar and a fraction of a percent of the window.

HEADLINE, wave 1, 24 runs: Sonnet is four to ten times FASTER than Haiku on the card task, which is the opposite of what everyone assumed. Median time to a finished card, minimal config: Sonnet low 2.92 s, medium 2.18 s, high 1.93 s (whole spread 1.8 to 3.0 s). Haiku low 11.95 s, medium 10.67 s, high 11.73 s (spread 5.3 to 34.5 s). Haiku is both slower and wildly unpredictable.

And the reason is one number. Sonnet 5 spent ZERO thinking tokens on this task at low, at medium and at high -- it judged the job not worth deliberating about. Haiku 4.5 spent a median of about 1000 thinking tokens and as many as 4009 on a single run, at LOW effort. Both models emit roughly 120 to 140 tokens a second, so the time is just the token count. Effort is a ceiling on thinking, not an instruction to think: the model decides whether to spend it, and on a small formatting job Sonnet decides not to.

CONCURRENCY, file writes, settled. Eight separate OS processes, released at the same millisecond by a spin barrier, appending whole JSON lines to one file: 12000 lines at 94 bytes, 12000 at 4 KB, and 2400 at 64 KB (150 MB of file) -- zero lines torn, zero lost, for all three of appendFileSync, writeSync on an append fd, and a createWriteStream in append mode. Appending a line is safe on this Windows machine at every size tested.

The same eight processes doing read-modify-write on one JSON file lost almost everything: 1576 of 1600 updates gone, 98.5 percent, and the file still parsed perfectly afterwards. That is the dangerous half -- nothing errors, nothing looks broken, the data is simply not there. The rule for a mastermind: agents may append lines to a shared file freely, and must never read-modify-write a shared file that another agent may touch.

Free usage meter found: every run emits a rate_limit_event carrying the live five-hour and seven-day utilization, so the window can be read off any call instead of hitting the usage endpoint. It also says overageStatus rejected, out_of_credits -- crossing 100 percent on this account is a hard stop, not a spillover.

The reason is one number: Sonnet spent ZERO thinking tokens on this job at every effort level, Haiku spent a median of ~1000 and up to 4009 at LOW. Effort is a ceiling on thinking, not an instruction to think -- and it does reach the model (Haiku, same task: low 5.30 s / 1060 thinking tokens, max 14.73 s / 2.8x the output). 2) Concurrency is settled: eight OS processes released on the same millisecond appended 12000 lines at 94 B, 12000 at 4 KB and 2400 at 64 KB to one file with ZERO torn or lost lines, for three different append APIs. The same eight doing read-modify-write on one JSON file lost 1576 of 1600 updates -- 98.5 percent -- and the file still parsed perfectly. **The rule: agents may append lines to a shared file freely, and must never read-modify-write a shared file another agent may touch.** Also found: every headless run emits a rate_limit_event carrying live five-hour and seven-day utilization, so usage can be read off any call for free.
